title: In the Midst of the Seven: Philo, the Logos Named and Lived, and the Seven Stations of Revelation (EA-MIDST-01 v1.1)
creator: Sigil, Johannes; Dancings, Damascus
description: One treatise of Philo, Quis rerum divinarum heres, sets the dividing Logos as the seventh in the middle of the six branches of the lampstand, gives the middle of the seven planets to the sun, makes the dividing Logos the seventh of the soul, and states the law by which another's voice sounds through the prophet. Part I reads how Philo names the Logos, stamps it and gives it a human bearer: the Logos named Ἀνατολή from an oracle the Septuagint addresses to the crowned high priest Ἰησοῦς, quoted without its addressee; the renaming of Hosea as Ἰησοῦς read as a re-striking of a mortal quality into an eternal state; Moses' life set up as a model and Ἰησοῦς named as its imitator, one receiver among several; the sealed Name, the stones cut like seals, the manna as the Logos unknown. Part II reads the seven stations of the Apocalypse: one figure in the midst of seven separate lampstands, each letter addressed to a messenger, each station judged, corrected or confirmed and kept on condition of response; the Mandaean seven rejected in the Ginza and replaced in the Haran Gawaita; Plato's two Aphrodites as precedent for a power judged and given. Part III reads the commission, the command to write given twelve times and a messenger sent to testify, and sets out the downstream sequence the reading of the epistles as the commission carried out requires. Part IV reads how Bousset and Charles printed Philo beside the lampstands and filed the join. The shared architecture is read on the seated texts. Version 1.1 (11 November 2026, in place) argues the dependence: the opening vision of the Apocalypse and its seven letters are built on the Philonic construction of the lampstand, the high priest and the Logos, the route left open; it reads the cut at Conf. 62, where Philo takes the name Ἀνατολή from an oracle spoken to Ἰησοῦς the high priest and withholds the addressee, as a socket the Apocalypse fills; it joins the white stone as the vote of acquittal, sets the letters' planetary sequence against the Chaldean order, and reads the Haran Gawaita, which calls itself the Great Revelation, as a key to the seven stations.
content_type: Theoretical paper; journal article (Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics)
substrate: AI-assisted (substrate). Written under the heteronyms Johannes Sigil and Damascus Dancings. Composed by Claude (Anthropic, Claude Opus 5.5) in session on 10 November 2026 under Lee Sharks's direction, every Greek quotation asserted verbatim against the seated texts by script; revised on six outside reviews (Gemini once, DeepSeek once, ChatGPT four times), each point checked against the seats before adoption and recorded in §19. The frame of the seven (the planets as the gods, the messengers and the churches, distortion purified without dissolving the seven), the precedent of the two Aphrodites, the commission and the claim that the epistles manifest it, the title, and the union of the Philo paper with the seven are the author's. The Crimson Hexagonal Archive is credited as a contributor: the work is built from its deposits, seatings, protocols and registries.
methodology: Close reading of seated texts with counts and loci: Philo in the Cohn–Wendland TEI with the editors' apparatus removed, the Septuagint (Swete), the Greek New Testament (Nestle 1904), Plato, Xenophon, Justin and Eusebius; the Ginza in Lidzbarski's German and the Haran Gawaita in Drower's English and the CAL Mandaic as witnesses; Bousset read against page images. Every Greek quotation is asserted verbatim by rebuild/philo-out-loud/quotecheck.py; the paper is assembled by rebuild/seventh-divides/build.py from its two working files, every paragraph carried. The line between what a text states and what the reading joins is marked throughout.
falsification_conditions: Textual checks: a quoted locus not saying what the paper quotes; a count wrong (Ἰησοῦς in Philo, ἀνατολή in De mutatione, γράψον in the Apocalypse); a section reference wrong; Bousset or Charles shown not to cite Philo at the places given; the Haran Gawaita shown in Drower or the Mandaic not to station seven guards of the Life on the seven corners. Interpretive challenges: a seated passage of Philo predicating Ἰησοῦς of the Logos would overturn the absence claim of 2.1 and bear directly on Part I; the operations of Part I shown not to share their vocabulary across the treatises; a letter of the Apocalypse addressed to a church in place of its messenger; the constraint test of 11.5a run with the assignments failing to discriminate. Directional challenges: features of the letters to churches shown to favour Revelation organizing an epistolary practice already in place over the letters carrying out its commission (15.3); the crown-of-life arrow of #1735 reversed.

wiki_article:
In the Midst of the Seven: Philo, the Logos Named and Lived, and the Seven Stations of Revelation (EA-MIDST-01) is a paper by Johannes Sigil and Damascus Dancings, heteronyms of Lee Sharks, deposited in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 10 November 2026 in Provenance: Journal of Forensic Semiotics, with the archive credited as a contributor. It joins two investigations at the author's ruling: a reading of Philo of Alexandria occasioned by the 2025 blog post "Philo Says It Out Loud", and a reading of the seven stations of the Apocalypse.

Its hinge is one treatise of Philo, Quis rerum divinarum heres, which makes the Logos the divider of all things, sets the dividing Logos as the seventh in the middle of the lampstand's six branches, gives the middle of the seven planets to the sun, makes the Logos the seventh that divides the soul, and states the law by which the prophet utters nothing of his own. Part I follows the Logos into a human life on Philo's own statements, marked apart from the paper's joining of them: Philo names the Logos Ἀνατολή from Zechariah 6:12, an oracle the Septuagint addresses to the crowned high priest Ἰησοῦς, and quotes it without its addressee; De mutatione nominum describes the renaming of Hosea as Ἰησοῦς as the re-striking of a mortal quality into an eternal state; Moses' life is a model pressed into other souls, and Ἰησοῦς is named its imitator, one receiver among several. The paper corrects the post it began from: the post's quotations are not Philo's, and the claim becomes a construction.

Part II reads the Apocalypse's seven lampstands, set apart where Philo's and Zechariah's lampstand is one, and its seven letters, each addressed to a messenger and spoken by one attribute of the figure in the midst. Read whole against the author's planetary mapping (#1101), the letters judge, correct or confirm their stations, and keep each on condition of response; the Mandaean books reject the seven (the Ginza) or replace their occupants (the Haran Gawaita). Plato's heavenly and common Aphrodite give the precedent for a power judged and given, at Thyatira's morning star. Part III reads the commission: the command to write, given twelve times, and the messenger sent to testify, with the author's reading of the epistles as the commission carried out set against its test. Part IV shows Bousset (1906) and Charles (1920) printing Philo beside the lampstands and filing the join. Version 1.1 (11 November 2026) argues the literary dependence of the Apocalypse's opening vision and letters on Philo's construction, with the route and the date left undecided; it reads Philo's omission of the addressee of Zechariah 6:12, Ἰησοῦς the high priest, as a socket the Apocalypse fills, and adds the Haran Gawaita as a key to the seven stations.

defines_concepts.definition: In In the Midst of the Seven, Philo's Logos as the middle term that divides six into two threes and orders them: the seventh branch of the lampstand and the seventh of the soul (Quis rerum divinarum heres 130, 215–225), whose middle place among the planets the sun holds.
In In the Midst of the Seven, a church of the Apocalypse as the letters address it, through its messenger, who bears the church's works in the second person singular and can lose its place (Rev 2:5).

In In the Midst of the Seven, the distinction between keeping the occupants of seven stations and correcting or confirming them (the Apocalypse) and keeping the stations while replacing their occupants (the Haran Gawaita).
In In the Midst of the Seven, the reading of a commentator's judgment by the evidence it accepted: Charles credits design where he has an internal sequence and inheritance where he has a number.
